did_you_know.text: Did you know? Jehoiakim was subject to Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, for three years, and then rebelled against him.

Did you know? Following Jehoiakim’s rebellion, the LORD sent bands of Chaldeans, Arameans, Moabites, and Ammonites against Judah, and Scripture presents this as the fulfillment of the prophets’ words.
Did you know? The Book of Kings explains that the calamity that befell Judah was also connected to Manasseh’s sins, describing it as the removal of Judah from the LORD’s presence.
Did you know? Alongside Manasseh’s sins, the shedding of innocent blood is also mentioned—a crime that filled Jerusalem with blood. According to Scripture, the LORD was unwilling to forgive it.
Did you know? During this period, the king of Egypt lost control of the region, and the king of Babylon took possession of the territory from the Brook of Egypt to the Euphrates River.
Did you know? Jehoiachin became king at the age of eighteen and reigned in Jerusalem for only three months; his mother was Nehushta, daughter of Elnathan.

Did you know? When the Babylonians besieged Jerusalem, Jehoiachin went out to the king of Babylon with his mother, servants, officials, and eunuchs, and he was taken captive in the eighth year of Nebuchadnezzar’s reign.

Did you know? Nebuchadnezzar carried away the treasures of the LORD’s temple and the treasures of the royal palace from Jerusalem, and he cut up the gold furnishings that Solomon had made for the temple of the LORD.
Did you know? Among those deported from Jerusalem were the officials, warriors, craftsmen, and smiths; according to Scripture, only the poorest people of the land remained.
Did you know? After Jehoiachin was deported, the king of Babylon appointed Jehoiachin’s uncle Mattaniah as king and changed his name to Zedekiah.
Did you know? In the end, Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon, even though it was the king of Babylon who had appointed him king in Jerusalem.
